summary:
Haiti has not criminalised same-sex conduct since 1791, but the legal framework provides no recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime enhancement. The judiciary does not function as a protection avenue in practice, so a trans visitor has no statutory remedy to invoke and no aggravated-penalty framework behind any complaint.

Two Senate measures would tighten the regime. In August 2017 the Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy, carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of about US$8,000 for the parties. A June 2017 bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs, the good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require, on grounds of homosexuality. As of November 2017 both awaited a vote in the Chamber of Deputies.

Visibility carries risk. The US State Department's 2018 report found that attitudes in Haiti remained hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince. In November 2019 Charlot Jeudy, president of the national advocacy organisation Kouraj, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince; reports of poisoning were unconfirmed. The regional network ILGALAC issued a mourning statement.

Transgender people have faced documented harassment in the post-earthquake camps. No prison-placement practice is documented for trans detainees: no rule assigns housing by birth sex or by identity, no separate units are recorded for them, and no solitary or segregation practice is recorded.
tangentialFactors:
With no hate-crime enhancement on the books, violence against trans people is handled under general criminal law, with no aggravating category tied to the victim's gender identity or sexual orientation.

Regional advocacy networks have responded to violence against Haitian LGBT figures. ILGALAC issued a mourning statement after Jeudy's death, and Kouraj operates as the national advocacy organisation.
localsOnly:
The Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs is required by many employers and schools, and it lists homosexuality as a crime that can justify denial of the certificate, which directly affects youth and students. A June 2017 Senate bill sought to regulate who receives this certification.

LGBTQ people in Haiti often conceal their orientation or gender identity for fear of discrimination, which impedes access to the constitutional guarantees of health care, housing, education, food and social security that apply to all citizens. The 1987 Constitution guarantees all citizens a right to education, though LGBTQ youth face pervasive social hostility.

After the 2010 earthquake, gay and bisexual men reported adopting a more masculine demeanor to avoid harassment and to reduce the chance of being denied emergency housing, healthcare and food-for-work programmes.

HIV infection rates in Haiti rose to 4 to 6 percent as of 2008, and to 13 percent in certain rural neighbourhoods. Grasadis, founded in 1997, works to prevent the spread of HIV/AIDS among the LGBTQ minority.
outOfScopeNotes:
Reports that Charlot Jeudy was poisoned were unconfirmed.

The status of the two 2017 Senate bills after November 2017 is not sourced. Whether they passed the Chamber of Deputies, lapsed or remain pending is unresolved.

No prison-placement rule for trans detainees is documented either way; the absence of a documented practice is not evidence that no practice exists.

The HIV prevalence figures date to 2008 and no current data is in the inventory.
